q: Focusing on difficult students, checking in on them, using proximity with them, and otherwise spending more time with them than your other students are all forms of labeling.
When you treat challenging students like everyone else, they tend to behave like everyone else.
Difficult students have been praised so often and for so long that it’s lost all its meaning.
Never tiptoe around difficult students or be fearful of holding them accountable. These, too, are labeling behaviors that can also give them a sense of entitlement.
You can build strong rapport with difficult students by just allowing them to enjoy being a regular student.
In most cases, difficult students don’t need a counselor. They need a leader and role model who sees their worth and potential and treats them as if they really can do it.

q: The next time you’re tempted to say yes to sponsoring a club, pursuing a degree, joining a committee, or reading a book, ask yourself: If I couldn’t tell a soul about this, would I still do it?

But the thing is, if I sponsor the club or read the book or get the PhD partly so that I can tell people about it or so that people will respect me or so that I won’t feel guilty — in short, if I do things in service of me — then I’m going to make decisions that poorly align with my life’s key objectives, and these decisions will pick away at my soul as they extract whatever hours of labor they cost.

I went and took a naturally good thing — reading — and I attached these artificial, ego-centered contraptions onto it, and made it something less. Reading stopped being about knowledge-building, pleasure, research, or wisdom, and it started being something about pressure and performance.

I don’t know who will sponsor the club — perhaps someone whose objective at school has something to do with the club. The junior class will persevere — surely some adult in the community will be able to guide them in their quest to plan prom.

And your boss will only think poorly of you if he or she views the purpose of school vaguely. People like you and me seek to make our bosses look good by focusing on the core mission of the school while living peaceably with the students, parents, and colleagues we work with.
I’m no creator of time. It all has to come from somewhere, and a day is coming when it’ll run out. Might as well use it on something much bigger than me.
x: His own example is a public reading challenge that turned a good habit into pressure and performance, and a second is the familiar pressure on teachers to sponsor a club for fear of what the boss or students will think.
The argument is that ego-driven yeses misalign with a person's real objectives and quietly cost the finite hours of a life, which are better spent on something bigger than oneself.
Attaching social display to a good activity, as with the public reading challenge, can turn it into pressure and performance.
Stuart offers a single decision test for commitments: ask whether you would still do something if you could tell no one about it.
Saying no to a club sponsorship is defended as aligning with the school's core mission, which good leaders protect rather than their own image.
Time is finite and has to be spent somewhere, so ego-driven commitments crowd out the work and home life that matter most.

t: My Number One Goal On The First Day Of School
q: My number one goal on the first day of school is that my students love being in my class.
You trigger the Law of Reciprocity, which causes them to want to repay you for creating a classroom they’re happy to be part of.
Emphasize that your classroom management plan is for them , not you, and it’s sole purpose is to protect their right to learn and enjoy school without being bothered, bullied, or interrupted.
Teach at least one routine—like entering the classroom or lining up for lunch—with the same energy and commitment you would the xy-graph, the scientific method, or the very fundamentals of grammar.
Children as young as five recognize great teaching when they see it, and they’re changed by it.
x: Argues that student enjoyment creates leverage, triggers reciprocity, and causes families to become supportive from day one.
Argues that student enjoyment creates leverage, triggers reciprocity, and causes families to become supportive from day one.
Advises framing the classroom management plan explicitly as existing for students' benefit, to protect their right to learn without interruption.
Recommends teaching at least one routine on day one with the same rigor and energy given to core academic content.
Linsin reveals that his top priority on the first day of school is not routines or the management plan itself, but making students genuinely love being in his class.

t: Here’s How to Overcome Student Speaking Anxiety
q: But students’ minds needn’t be stone cold on a question before you call on them. Rather, I find it’s best to have students first answer a question (briefly) in writing, and then to have them share the gist of what they’ve written with a peer, and then to work through your roster calling them at random.

Normalize participation early and often. As Martha Sevetson Rush writes in Beat Boredom: Engaging Tuned-Out Teenagers, “Once a classroom culture is established, it is difficult to change, so lecturing for six weeks and then suddenly calling on students to discuss will result in an uncomfortable silence” (73).

Once a student indicates to me that they are anxious about speaking publicly (as Kym did via email, or this past year as Chris did when he refused to speak during a Week 1 warm-call), I take extra pains to connect with them via moments of genuine connection. My goal is to make them feel valued, known, and respected.
Where possible, I speak to their anxiety around public speaking during these moments, and about how this is actually normal. I sometimes share how this was my own struggle in school, too.
I’m explicit before the debate starts: this will happen! And all you need to do in this situation is read from the writing you did at the start of class.
This is a weird thing about anxiety — it convinces us that we’re the only ones experiencing it! But actually, it is normal to feel some trepidation about speaking in front of one’s peers.
x: Warm-calling, with a short written answer and a peer share before the teacher calls on someone at random, gets every student speaking in week one without cold shock.
Participation norms have to be set early, because a classroom culture that is established around silence is hard to change later.

Anxious students need targeted connection and advance coaching, such as being told success is simply reading their warm-up writing aloud.
Stuart tells the story of Kym, a ninth grader convinced she could not speak in class, to lay out a seven-step approach to student public-speaking anxiety.

q: Chip away at sleep debt rather than trying to pay it off one morning a week. It’s better to add 30 minutes to each night of sleep for a week than to add 4 hours to one night of sleep once per week.
Nappucinos work. This is the thing where right before that afternoon slump hits, you down a cup of coffee and then lay down and shut your eyes for fifteen minutes.
Treat yourself like an organism that you are studying. Jim Collins used to keep a “bug book” on himself, studying himself to try to understand what he should do with his life.
I wouldn’t like to see the number of times that I’ve taken a “break” from work by checking email or Twitter or the news or YouTube. This is dumb.
Instead, take a walk, do some jumping jacks, stare at a window, do a nappucino, call your grandma… do something besides the digital default.

Thanks to headphones and podcasts and Spotify and car radio and audiobooks, it’s easy to ensure that every moment of our day is filled with stimuli. I’ve found it quite liberating to intentionally not use stimuli at various points in the day.

All of these can seem a bit nit-picky when you look at them, like a list of buzz-killing joy-stealers. But I’ve found the opposite to be true: when I operate beneath a few simple, logical rules like these, I end up experiencing more freedom and creative output, and I end up giving more to others.
x: Sleep debt is better repaid in small nightly additions than in a single long catch-up night, a habit Jim Collins tracks by totaling recent hours.
Stuart shares nine practices he adopted over a summer to protect his energy for work, family and play, drawing on Jim Collins, Make Time, Dan Pink and Brigid Schulte.

The tips include chipping away at sleep debt in small nightly increments, using a coffee-then-nap routine, logging daily energy like a researcher studying himself, and keeping a list of people who energize you.
Fake breaks like email and social feeds trade one demanding mental task for another, while real breaks use movement, quiet or rest.

q: Last time, I discussed how critical thinking is not the “holy grail” transferrable skill that we tend to think it is. Rather, it is a function of knowledge, something most deeply practicable in domains we know enough about.

When faced with a day’s lesson, who is going to find it easier to believe that they can succeed — all other things being equal? The Efficacy belief will be easier for Student A, simply because Student A is actually going to have a much easier time succeeding!

Conversely, Student B might have a wonderful relationship with the teacher and a great social connection with her peers, but when it’s time to get to the work of learning Algebra, she’s going to doubt whether or not she fits in with the rest of the class simply because she lacks the prior knowledge that the class requires.
Sometimes, the biggest motivational obstacle for the students in our classes is that they just don’t know enough. This lack of knowledge creates doubt and fear.

And this all sounds like bad news, but actually it’s the opposite. When we can identify that a student’s lack of motivation is stemming from a lack of prior knowledge, we now know exactly what we need to do next.
We don’t need to blame or label or pathologize the student. Instead, we can teach them.
x: Following his argument that critical thinking is a function of knowledge, Stuart extends the idea to motivation.
Prior knowledge underlies the efficacy belief, since a student who already has the prerequisites will find it much easier to believe she can succeed.
Belonging is also knowledge-dependent: a student who cannot follow the work will doubt she fits in, even with strong peer and teacher relationships.
Belonging is also knowledge-dependent: a student who cannot follow the work will doubt she fits in, even with strong peer and teacher relationships.
The reframing is that many motivation problems are actually knowledge problems.
That is good news, because the teacher's response becomes teaching rather than blaming, labeling or pathologizing the student.

q: It’s common to confuse rules with encouragements—which are behaviors you’d like to see in your students but are ultimately unenforceable.
Do your best. Be ready to learn. Try new things. Have fun. Dream big. Make wise choices.
Rules protect your freedom to teach and your students’ right to learn and enjoy school. That’s it.
Encouragements like those listed above, on the other hand, do no such thing and are all but impossible to enforce.
They’re also incredibly confusing to students—and hurtful if you do attempt to enforce them.
Some readers even discovered that none of their rules covered actual disruptions.
x: Warns that attempting to enforce encouragements as rules is confusing and can be hurtful to students.
Building on a previous exercise, Linsin explains a subtle problem some readers discovered: rules that don't actually cover any real disruptions because they're really encouragements.
Encouragements, by contrast, are confusing to students and can be hurtful if a teacher tries to enforce them as though they were rules.

q: I stood up and brought the debate to a close, thanking students for their participation thus far and saying that I’d give more articles in the future to help us understand the crisis at a deeper level.

This time, even my shyest students participated in the debate before I could call on them, and not a single student suggested that the United States conduct a nuclear strike on the peninsula. There was a clear sense in the room that North Korea is a place where people live, and that the matter is unsolved today precisely because of the complex historical and geopolitical factors.

For example, let’s say you ask me to think critically about the most pressing political issue in Kazakhstan. Today, you would find me a poor critical thinker on the matter; I simply lack the knowledge.
Critical thinking is not primarily a transferrable skill. It’s much more accurate to think of it as a byproduct of knowledge.

Who is the better one to ask a tough question about teaching: first-year Dave or tenth-year Dave? Definitely tenth-year Dave — not because his IQ has improved, but because his capacity for deep, clear, discerning, critical thought within the domain of teaching has improved.

I share these things to help us break away from the illogical, unsupported notion that critical thinking is something detachable from robust knowledge-building. We must stop thinking of knowledge-building as a rote and boring thing, and instead start to think of it as an integral part of learning anything.
x: The same debate went far better, with students recognizing the issue's complexity.

Stuart opens with a failed pop-up debate in which several ninth graders recommended a nuclear strike on North Korea, then shows what changed after four weeks of modest reading and short videos on the topic.
From this he argues that critical thinking is less a transferable skill than a byproduct of knowledge in a particular domain.
Critical thinking sharpens when students know more about the topic, so asking for thoughtful debate without giving background invites shallow answers.
The Kazakhstan and first-year versus tenth-year Dave examples show that expertise in a domain, not general IQ, drives discerning thought.
The practical move is to stop treating knowledge-building as rote and boring and to build small, efficient knowledge opportunities around the issues students are asked to think about.

t: The Effort Belief in Action: Read Naturally as a Case Study
q: His conviction wasn’t built on laziness or bad intentions. Nic, like all of the students I’ve ever taught, didn’t want to be unsuccessful, and in other realms of life he proved that his work ethic could be strong.

We seek to build it with vague praise — “Good job, you tried hard!” — rather than useful, targeted feedback. And we overestimate the power of effort while underemphasizing the critical roles of scaffolding, quality instruction, and prior knowledge in making effort efficacious.

The most difficult thing about building the effort belief in our students is that our students are not foolish. If students like Nic weren’t intelligent, then we could tell them to just keep trying, just keep putting in effort, just keep believing in themselves, and they’d just keep putting in effort.
But Nic’s not dumb, and so he needs to see that effort works. He needs some indication that trying will actually change things.

When they do pass, they graph their new score onto the same bar with their initial, unpracticed score, using a different colored pencil or marker. This graph gives tangible evidence to the students that they are improving—and keeps motivation high by showing them that their own effort makes the difference.

Perhaps the most important thing to understand about the effort belief is that it can’t cure poor instructional design. A central question of the educator’s work is, “How do I actually teach this thing? How do I actually help students get better at X?
The five key beliefs are the simplest way I know for understanding what makes motivated learners tick and unmotivated learners… untick. But just because they are simple doesn’t mean they are easy.
x: He closes by describing the deal he struck with Nic, flexing his own policies so the student could re-engage.

He argues that the popular idea of growth mindset has been misread as a fixed trait that can be built with vague praise, when it actually shifts with context and depends on scaffolding, good instruction and prior knowledge.
The effort belief cannot rescue weak instruction, so the teacher's first question remains how to actually help students get better at the thing.
Students who have years of evidence that effort does not pay will not be persuaded by encouragement; they need to see effort change results.
